title: Vantage Technology, LLC v. Cross
lead: A cataract-equipment technician used relationships developed while working for Vantage to enter the same business. Tennessee’s appellate court found a protectable interest but narrowed his covenant before remanding for a breach determination.

actors.name: Vantage Technology
actors.role: Supplier of mobile cataract-surgery equipment and technicians

actors.name: Cross
actors.role: Former Vantage technician who started a competing business

actors.name: Dr. Gollamudi
actors.role: Surgeon who helped finance Cross’s business

proceedings: After bench trial, chancellor held covenant unenforceable.
Court of Appeals reversed that determination, narrowed the restriction, and remanded for breach and relief.
Denial of loyalty-claim amendment and application of Tennessee law affirmed.
limits: Historical covenant decision. No damages or hospital-specific breach determination was made on appeal; classroom mileage figures are hypothetical, not findings.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Vantage develops technicians and customer relationships
paragraphs: Vantage Technology supplied rural hospitals with cataract-surgery equipment, supplies, and technicians. Surgeons’ preferences influenced both hospital choice and the mobile supplier hired. Vantage initiated relationships through sales efforts; technicians maintained them, transported and prepared equipment, and adjusted machine modes while surgeons operated. No medical license was required, and basic operation was quickly learned. Technicians nevertheless used and updated doctor diaries with machine settings, instrument preferences, and personal information, reported opportunities, and could entertain staff at company expense.

Cross joined in October 1994 without relevant training. His first month included 241.5 training hours, largely observing roughly seventy operations, followed by manuals, videos, meetings, and a wet lab. He served forty-nine hospitals in at least six states, used the diaries, and knew some pricing and contract information. By summer 1996 he was the main technician for many operations at Fort Sanders-Loudon and Lakeway and had developed a strong relationship with Dr. Gollamudi.

In January 1995 he signed a restriction on competition during employment and for three years afterward within fifty miles of any company office or client location. The agreement also called for enforcement to the extent allowed by the law of the jurisdiction where enforcement was sought, deleting invalid portions there.

sections.title: Cross enters the business
paragraphs: When Vantage proposed Ohio assignments in summer 1996, Cross and Gollamudi discussed an independent business using another machine the doctor preferred. Cross met LaFollette’s operating-room director August 13 without disclosing that he still worked for Vantage, gave two weeks’ notice August 15, and quoted LaFollette the next day. Gollamudi loaned him $40,000. Cross ordered a refurbished machine on his last employment day, August 29, and learned its operation from the manufacturer’s representative.

He began serving LaFollette September 10, Lakeway within a month, Fort Sanders-Loudon in October, and Fort Sanders-Sevierville in January 1997. Vantage had served LaFollette once in 1994 without establishing continuing business and first contacted Sevierville in April 1998. Vantage sued in May 1997 for contractual damages and an injunction. After a bench trial, the chancellor found its covenant unreasonable and unenforceable.

sections.title: An interest beyond ordinary competition
sections.cue: The appellate court changes the analysis
paragraphs: Judge Susano’s appellate opinion applied Tennessee’s strict construction of employment restraints while recognizing reasonable protection against unfair competitive advantages. General skill remained Cross’s, and public information was not protected just because Vantage possessed it. Specialized training, confidential information, and customer goodwill nevertheless had to be considered together.

The chancellor had discounted each factor separately. The appellate court found the evidence preponderated against that conclusion: Vantage trained Cross, initiated the relationships, placed him in an agency role maintaining them, and furnished preferences and business information. His relationship with Gollamudi particularly enabled competition at Vantage’s expense. A different machine or lack of continuing need for diaries did not negate the combined advantage. Threatened loss of those investments outweighed Cross’s hardship. Possible health-care cost increases did not overcome the interests in encouraging training and preventing exploitation of employer-created advantages.

The restraint still exceeded that interest. Surgeons’ nearby work justified fifty-mile areas around customer hospitals Cross had served, not company offices or hospitals he had never served. Without evidence of deliberately oppressive drafting, modification was appropriate. Ambiguities favored Cross: mileage meant the shortest driving route, and client locations meant hospitals receiving regular Vantage service when he departed. The court approved three years only within that narrowed territory.

sections.title: What remains for trial
paragraphs: On the first trial day, after four witnesses had testified, Vantage sought to add a loyalty claim based on Cross’s solicitation before notice. Denial was affirmed. Evidence about timing also concerned the pleaded covenant claim, so questioning on it did not establish implied consent to a new theory. Dismissed witnesses and lack of fair notice would impair Cross’s response. The ruling did not eliminate employees’ loyalty obligations.

The court also rejected Cross’s request for Illinois law. It gave separate effect to the clause’s choice-of-law sentence and severability sentence, finding good faith, a Tennessee connection, no sham, and no materially greater Illinois interest. Possible variation among enforcement forums did not defeat this particular clause; a proper final judgment would prevent relitigation between the parties.

The court reversed the covenant’s wholesale invalidation and remanded to determine whether Cross breached the modified restriction and, if so, what injunction or damages followed. It affirmed the amendment and governing-law rulings, divided appeal costs equally, and awarded no sum. Judge Goddard concurred; Judge Inman did not participate. Permission to appeal was later denied April 17, 2000.
